---
title: "The G431 ESC board"
---

Background on the **B-G431B-ESC1**, the board you rework and flash in
[Module 3](/sessions/03-esc.qmd). What is on it, how it turns a DC battery into
three moving phases, what it can drive, and why it arrives in two pieces.

## What it is

ST sells this as a *Discovery kit*: a reference design showing what their
STM32G431 can do in a motor-control role, in the physical form of a drone ESC.
That origin explains most of its oddities. A hobby ESC exposes a signal wire and
two power leads because that is all a flight controller needs; this board brings
out a CAN bus, a potentiometer input, a hall-sensor connector and a debug
header, because its job is to demonstrate everything the chip supports.

For us the consequence is good and bad in equal measure. Good: the silicon is
open, we can run our own firmware ([SimpleFOC](/reference/simple-foc.qmd)) and
we get real current sensing. Bad: several connectors are wired for uses we do
not want, which is why [Module 3](/sessions/03-esc.qmd) spends its time
repurposing them.

![The power stage. The six large flat packages are the MOSFETs, in three pairs; the copper tabs on the left are the U, V and W phase outputs.](/Fig/g431-power-stage.jpg){#fig-power-stage width="75%"}

## The parts that matter

| Block | Part | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Microcontroller | **STM32G431CB** | 170 MHz Cortex-M4 with FPU, 128 kB flash, 32 kB RAM |
| Power switches | **6 × STL180N6F7** | 60 V N-channel MOSFETs, very low on-resistance |
| Gate drivers | **L6387** | Three half-bridge drivers, one per phase |
| Current sensing | **Three shunts** | Low-side, amplified into the MCU's ADCs |
| Programmer | **ST-LINK/V2-1** | On the detachable daughterboard |

Sources: ST's [product page](https://www.st.com/en/evaluation-tools/b-g431b-esc1.html)
and data brief.

The MCU is the interesting choice. FOC recomputes the field orientation every
control loop, and each iteration costs a handful of trigonometric evaluations
(see [How SimpleFOC works](/reference/simple-foc.qmd)). At 170 MHz with hardware
floating point that fits comfortably inside a 10 kHz loop. A hobby ESC's 8-bit
microcontroller could not do this arithmetic in the time available, which is
precisely why hobby ESCs use the cruder back-EMF scheme instead.

## How the three phases are generated
The battery supplies one DC voltage. The motor needs three voltages that vary
smoothly and stay 120° apart. The bridge between the two is built from three
identical circuits.

**One half-bridge per phase.** Each phase output connects to two MOSFETs in
series across the battery: a **high-side** switch to the positive rail and a
**low-side** switch to ground. Closing the high side pulls that phase to battery
voltage; closing the low side pulls it to zero. Three phases, three pairs, six
transistors --- the six packages in @fig-power-stage.

**PWM makes the intermediate values.** A switch is either on or off, so a
half-bridge can only output the full rail or nothing. Switching between them
tens of thousands of times a second and varying the *fraction* of time spent
high produces any average voltage in between. 50% duty gives half the rail. The
motor's own winding inductance does the smoothing: it resists rapid current
changes, so it responds to the average and largely ignores the switching.

**Three of them, offset, make a rotating field.** Drive the three duty cycles as
sinusoids 120° apart and the three phase voltages produce a magnetic field that
sweeps steadily around the stator. Advance the sinusoids faster and the field
rotates faster. This is what `driver.setPwm(Ua, Ub, Uc)` at the bottom of
[SimpleFOC's inner loop](/reference/simple-foc.qmd) is ultimately setting.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Both switches in a pair must never be on together

High and low side closed at once is a direct short across the battery through
two transistors --- called **shoot-through**, and it destroys the pair in
microseconds. The hardware inserts a **dead time**: a brief interval where both
are off during every transition. It is handled by the gate drivers and the
MCU's timer, so you will not code it, but it is why the two switches of a pair
are never driven by a single signal.
:::

**Current sensing closes the loop.** A small-value **shunt resistor** sits in
each phase's low-side return path. The voltage across it is proportional to the
current through that phase; the MCU amplifies and samples it. Three shunts mean
all three phase currents are visible, which is what makes true FOC current
control possible rather than voltage-mode approximation. Without this
measurement you can ask for a torque; with it you can *regulate* one.

## What it can drive

| | |
|---|---|
| Input voltage | **3S to 6S** LiPo (roughly 11--25 V) |
| Peak current | **40 A**, with forced-air cooling |
| Protection | Overcurrent, overvoltage and thermal, on-board |

Two cautions about that 40 A. It is a **peak** figure, and it assumes **forced
air** --- a fan, or a drone's propwash. Our robot has neither, and it spends
much of its life underwater with the board sealed inside potting compound
([Module 10](/sessions/10-waterproofing.qmd)), so heat leaves slowly and only by
conduction. Treat 40 A as a number describing the silicon, not a budget you may
spend.

In practice this is not the binding constraint. The wing motor draws far less
than the board can supply, so the limits you will actually meet are the motor's
own thermal limit and sensor lag, not the ESC's. The relevant discussion is in
[Brushless motors](/reference/bldc.qmd) and
[Module 4](/sessions/04-control.qmd).

## Why there is a daughterboard

The small board at the end is a complete **ST-LINK/V2-1** programmer and debug
probe. It is separated from the power board by a line of perforations and is
meant to be snapped off.

That design makes sense for ST's intended user: develop with the programmer
attached, then break it away so the flight-ready ESC is smaller and lighter, and
reuse the same programmer on the next board. It carries two things:

- **SWD** --- the debug and programming interface, used to flash the MCU
- **A virtual COM port** --- a USB serial bridge onto one of the MCU's UARTs

::: {.callout-important}
## Do not snap it off

Once separated, reprogramming needs an external programmer wired to the SWD
pads by hand. We keep it attached for the whole course. This is also why the
board is larger than a hobby ESC of equivalent power --- roughly half of what
you are holding is the programmer.
:::

The virtual COM port is where [Module 3](/sessions/03-esc.qmd) runs into
trouble. Out of the box it is wired to the MCU's **USART2**, on pins that the
board also uses for the hall-sensor connector. Those same pins are the SPI3 bus
we need for the AS5047P encoder, and an encoder is not optional for FOC. So the
pins go to the encoder, USART2 stops being reachable over USB, and serial has to
be re-routed --- either onto USART1 by rework, or off-board entirely to the
Seeeduino. Flashing is unaffected throughout, because SWD runs on different
pins.

## What we do not use

- **CAN transceiver.** Present and functional; our robot uses BLE from the
  flight controller instead.
- **Potentiometer input.** An analog throttle knob for bench demonstrations.
- **Hall-sensor connector (J8).** Intended for the three digital hall sensors
  built into many BLDC motors. Ours has none, and hall sensors would be too
  coarse anyway --- six positions per electrical revolution, against the
  AS5047P's continuous absolute angle. The connector gets repurposed for serial.

Sources: [ST B-G431B-ESC1 product page](https://www.st.com/en/evaluation-tools/b-g431b-esc1.html),
[data brief](https://www.st.com/resource/en/data_brief/b-g431b-esc1.pdf).
